captions.text: In January 1920 a man in Boston
named Charles Ponzi started a firm called
the Securities Exchange Company
He promised clients a fifty percent profit
within forty-five days
In the first month eighteen
people invested a total of one thousand
eight hundred dollars
So how could a promise that big
fall apart so fast
Ponzi was born in Lugo in Italy
On the fifteenth of November 1903
he arrived in Boston aboard the steamship
Vancouver
By his own account
he had two dollars and fifty cents
in his pocket
Later he said he landed with two
dollars fifty in cash and a million
dollars in hopes
His story was that he bought international
reply coupons cheaply abroad and redeemed them
at face value in the United States
Between February and March 1920
the money invested rose from five thousand
to twenty-five thousand dollars
By late July
Ponzi was taking in two hundred and
fifty thousand dollars a day
But to cover the money a hundred
and sixty million coupons would have had
to exist
and only about twenty-seven thousand
did
On the twenty-sixth
of July 1920
the Boston Post started asking hard questions
Investors lost about twenty million dollars in
nineteen-twenty money
Charged with eighty-six counts of mail fraud
Ponzi was sentenced to five years in
federal prison
Released in 1934
he told reporters that he went looking
for trouble and found it
He died in Rio de Janeiro in
leaving an estate of seventy-five dollars Would
you have trusted a promise of fifty
percent in forty-five days
